questions.q: What happens if an exception is raised and there's no try/except around it?
options: The entire program crashes, and nothing after that line runs
Python silently ignores the error and continues
Python automatically retries the operation three times
The program pauses until the user presses a key
questions.explain: An unhandled exception stops the program immediately — that's exactly what try/except prevents.

questions.q: What does wrapping risky code in try/except actually do?
options: It makes the code run faster
It prevents the risky code from ever being run
It runs the risky code, and if it raises the matching exception, the except block handles it so the program keeps running
It converts all errors into warnings automatically
questions.explain: try runs the code; except catches a matching exception so execution continues instead of crashing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend catching specific exception types instead of a bare `except:`?
options: There is no difference between the two approaches
Specific exceptions run slower than catching everything
Python doesn't allow catching specific exception types
A bare except: hides real bugs along with the expected failures you meant to catch
questions.explain: Catching everything blindly can mask genuine bugs that should be visible, not silently swallowed.

Is not valid Python syntax
Runs regardless of whether an exception happened or not — useful for cleanup

questions.explain: finally always executes, whether the try block succeeded or an exception was caught.

questions.q: What does `raise ValueError("prompt cannot be empty")` do inside a function?
options: Has no effect unless wrapped in a print statement
Automatically fixes the empty prompt problem
Logs a warning but lets the function continue running normally
Signals a specific error condition, stopping execution and handing a clear message up to the caller
questions.explain: raise deliberately triggers an exception with a specific message, which is far more useful than a confusing failure later.
